notes.summary: Figural questions use shapes instead of words: what comes next in a series, what completes an analogy or a pattern, which figure is the odd one out, how a figure looks after rotating, and which option hides a given figure. The method is always the same: break the figure into parts (shape, number, position, direction, shading) and track how each part changes.

concepts.title: Break the figure into parts
concepts.body:
Most figures change in one or two ways at once. List the parts and watch each one separately:
PartHow it usually changes
DirectionTurns 45°, 90° or 180°, clockwise or anticlockwise
PositionMoves 1, 2 or 3 corners or sides at a time
NumberLines, dots or sides go up or down by 1 (or 1, 2, 3)
ShadingFilled and empty take turns
ShapeInner and outer shapes swap, or sides increase

concepts.title: Rotation basics
concepts.body:
• Clockwise is the way clock hands move; anticlockwise is the other way.
  • 90° clockwise is the same as 270° anticlockwise. 180° is the same both ways.
  • Combine turns into one net turn: 135° clockwise then 45° anticlockwise = 90° clockwise.
  • A rotated figure never becomes its mirror image. If a shape has flipped, it was reflected, not rotated.

In the figure: turning the flag 90° clockwise lays the pole flat with the flag at the right end, pointing down.

concepts.title: Figure series
concepts.body:
Find the change from figure 1 to 2, check it holds from 2 to 3 and 3 to 4, then apply it once more.
  • Steps can grow: a dot may move 1, then 2, then 3 places.
  • An element moving around n positions is back at the start after n steps.
  • If two parts move, track them one at a time and combine at the end.

In the figure: the arrow turns 45° anticlockwise each time, so the next one points down to the left.

concepts.title: Figure analogy
concepts.body:
Write down every change from A to B (rotation, shading, count, inside or outside), then apply exactly the same changes to C.

In the figure: an empty triangle (3 sides) becomes a filled square (4 sides). So the empty pentagon (5 sides) becomes a filled hexagon (6 sides).

concepts.title: Odd figure out
concepts.body:
Three figures share a rule; one breaks it. Common rules: all are rotations of the same shape (the odd one is a mirror image), all have the same number of lines or sides, or all have the same shading pattern.

In the figure: (a), (b) and (d) are the same L turned through 0°, 90° and 180°. (c) is flipped, a mirror image, so it is the odd one.

concepts.title: Completing a pattern
concepts.body:
Most such figures are symmetric: left matches right, top matches bottom, or each quarter is a turned copy of the next. Continue every line that reaches the edge of the gap, and check that the piece you choose has the right curves and slants.

In the figure: the missing quarter must hold a quarter of the circle and the diagonal from the centre to the bottom-right corner.

concepts.title: Embedded figures
concepts.body:
The hidden figure must appear with the same size, shape and angle; rotation and flipping are not allowed unless stated.
  1. Note one special feature of X: a slanted line, a right angle at one corner, a small loop.
  2. Look for that feature in each option, at the same angle.
  3. Trace the rest of X from there. Every line of X must be present.

In the figure: X is a right triangle with the right angle at the bottom left. Option (a) contains it (below its diagonal). In (b) the diagonal slants the other way, so the triangles there have the right angle at a different corner.

varieties.name: Embedded figure
varieties.how: Pick one special feature of X, find it at the same angle in an option, then trace every line of X. No rotating or flipping.

example.q: Which option contains figure X as a part (rotation not allowed)?
steps: X is a right triangle with the right angle at the bottom left and the long side slanting down from top left to bottom right.
(a) is a square with a diagonal from top left to bottom right; its lower half is exactly X.
(b) has the other diagonal, so its triangles have the right angle at the top left or bottom right.

varieties.name: Completing a pattern
varieties.how: Use the symmetry of the whole figure and continue every line that reaches the gap.

steps: The figure is a square with both diagonals and a circle centred in it.
The other three quarters each hold a quarter circle and a half-diagonal.
So the gap needs a quarter of the circle and the line from the centre to the bottom-right corner.
example.answer: The quarter with a circle arc and a diagonal from the centre to the corner

varieties.name: Figure series
varieties.how: Find the change between neighbours, check it across the row, then apply it once more.

example.q: Which figure comes next in the series?
steps: Figure 1 points up, figure 2 up-left, figure 3 left.
Each step is a 45° turn anticlockwise.
One more 45° anticlockwise turn from left gives down-left.
example.answer: The arrow pointing down to the left

varieties.name: Figure analogy
varieties.how: List every change from A to B and apply the same changes to C.

example.q: Find the figure that completes the analogy.
steps: A is an empty triangle (3 sides); B is a filled square (4 sides).
Rule: one more side, and the shape becomes filled.
C is an empty pentagon (5 sides), so D has 6 sides and is filled.

varieties.name: Odd figure out
varieties.how: Find the rule three figures share, often "same shape turned", and pick the one that breaks it, often a mirror image.

example.q: Which figure is the odd one out?
steps: (a) is an L with its foot to the right.
(b) and (d) are the same L turned 90° and 180°.
(c) has its foot to the left with the long arm upright: it is a mirror image, which no rotation can produce.

varieties.name: Rotating a figure
varieties.how: Combine all turns into one net turn (clockwise minus anticlockwise), then turn one clear feature of the figure.

example.q: The flag is rotated 135° clockwise and then 45° anticlockwise. How does it look?
steps: The top of the pole moves to the right, so the pole lies flat with the flag at the right end.
The flag pointed right; after 90° clockwise it points down.
example.answer: Pole flat, flag at the right end pointing down

tips: Track one part at a time: direction, position, number, shading, shape.
Combine rotations into one net turn before you look at the options.
A mirror image can never be made by rotating; use this to spot odd ones out.
In series, check that the change holds for every step, not just the first.
In embedded figures, start from the most unusual line of X.
Eliminate options that break even one part of the rule.
traps: Do not rotate the option figures in embedded questions when rotation is not allowed.
A 90° clockwise turn and a 90° anticlockwise turn give different figures; check the direction.
Two changes can happen at once (rotation and shading); an option that gets only one right is a trap.
Elements moving around a square can move by different steps each time (1, 2, 3).

questions.q: Select the figure that will come next in the given series.
questions.solution:
The arrow turns 45° clockwise at each step: up → up-right → right → down-right.
Next: another 45° clockwise → pointing straight down: option (b).

questions.q: Select the figure that is related to the third figure in the same way as the second figure is related to the first figure.
questions.solution:
Figure 1: big circle with a small square inside. Figure 2: big square with a small circle inside.
Rule: the outer and inner shapes swap.
Figure 3: big triangle with a small circle → big circle with a small triangle: option (c).

questions.q: Select the figure that will come next in the given series.
questions.solution:
Dot: moves one corner clockwise each step (top-left → top-right → bottom-right → bottom-left), so next it returns to top-left.
Lines: 1, 2, 3, 4 → next 5.
Option (d): dot at top-left with 5 lines.

questions.q: Select the figure that is related to the third figure in the same way as the second figure is related to the first figure.
questions.solution:
The upward arrow becomes a right-pointing arrow: a 90° clockwise rotation.
Rotate the flag 90° clockwise: the pole becomes horizontal with the flag at the right end, pointing down, and the base at the left: option (d).
(a) is 90° anticlockwise, (b) is a mirror image and (c) is 180°.

questions.q: Select the option figure that is embedded in the given figure (rotation is not allowed).
questions.solution:
The figure has: the outer square, one diagonal from top-left to bottom-right, a vertical middle line, and a horizontal middle line on the right half only.
(c) a small square with a top-left to bottom-right diagonal = the bottom-right quarter of the figure ✓.
(a) needs the other diagonal ✗. (b) needs a steep slanted line ✗. (d) needs a line from top-right to bottom-left ✗.

questions.q: Select the option figure that is embedded in the given figure (rotation is not allowed).
questions.solution:
The figure has: the outer square, the diagonal from top-right to bottom-left, and a shorter parallel line cutting off the top-left corner.
(b) is the strip between the two slanted lines, closed by part of the top side and part of the left side ✓.
(a) is the mirror image (slants the other way) ✗. (c) needs a slanted line near the bottom-right corner ✗. (d) needs the top-left to bottom-right diagonal ✗.

flashcards.back: Track each element (rotation, position, count) separately.
Same size and same orientation; every line must exist in the figure.
